extracted.intended_audience: readers of Pascal / students of theology and apologetics; general educated readers interested in religious argumentation
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Pascal's criteria for judging the truth, authenticity, and divine origin of religions and scriptures (especially Christianity and Judaism), using historical, textual, moral, and phenomenological signs. Focuses on permanence, prophecy, miracles, sincerity of witnesses, clarity/obscurity, and related comparative tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural double meaning / concealed spiritual meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: 'This meaning is concealed under another in an infinite number of passages, and in some, though rarely, it is revealed; but yet so that the passages in which it is concealed are equivocal, and can suit both meanings; whereas the passages where it is disclosed are unequivocal, and can only suit the spiritual meaning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal treats the presence of dual (literal and spiritual) senses as intentional: concealed (equivocal) passages can be read both ways while disclosed passages are unequivocal; this balance prevents certain errors and is meaningful for interpretation (those with worldly covetousness will misunderstand concealed spiritual meanings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motives: covetousness vs charity as interpretive criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There are two principles, which divide the wills of men, covetousness and charity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate readers' and interpreters' motives: covetousness limits meaning to worldly goods and leads to error; charity (love of God) leads to seeing spiritual meanings. Pascal uses moral disposition as a criterion for who correctly apprehends scripture and blessings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of clearness and obscurity in Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is sufficient clearness to enlighten the elect, and sufficient obscurity to humble them. There is sufficient obscurity to blind the reprobate, and sufficient clearness to condemn them, and make them inexcusable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal sees a deliberate balance — some passages are clear enough to convince the elect; obscurities humble the faithful and expose the reprobate. Use presence of both clear fulfilled prophecies and obscurities as evidence of divine design rather than human manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divine use of obscurity to humble pride and preserve the will
rubrics_metrics.description: 'God prefers rather to incline the will than the intellect. Perfect clearness would be of use to the intellect, and would harm the will. To humble pride.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opacity in revelation is presented as purposeful: too much intellectual clarity would subvert free will or foster pride. Apparent contradictions or difficult passages may be signs of a providential design to test and form moral character; apparent weaknesses may be strengths intended to prevent pride or heresy.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Blindness of Scripture' as explanation for unbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: 'They believed not, though He had done so many miracles, that the word of Isaiah might be fulfilled: "He hath blinded them"'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unbelief despite miracles is interpreted as divinely permitted blindness fulfilling prophecy. Lack of belief in witnesses or miracles is therefore not decisive against truth, since scripture explains the phenomenon as part of providence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetuity / antiquity of a religion or people as evidential sign
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That religion has always existed on earth... All things have passed away, and this has endured, for which all things are.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longstanding, continuous existence (perpetuity) of a religion or people — especially the Jewish people and their law/book — is used as positive evidence of divine origin. Pascal argues that the antiquity and uninterrupted duration of Jewish religion/law distinguish it from transient sects and support Christianity's foundation upon it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fulfilment of prophecy as proof
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The prophecies being thereby fulfilled, the Messiah is for ever proved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific prophecies (their content, time, and manner) fulfilled in history are treated as decisive evidence for the truth of a religion that predicted them. Pascal emphasizes prophecy that is clear and manifestly fulfilled rather than merely obscure parallels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles of Christ and the Apostles as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Jesus Christ performed miracles, and the Apostles also, who converted all the heathen.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporaneous miracles and the extraordinary effects of apostleship (conversion of many) serve as signs of divine endorsement. Pascal regards miracles as part of the chain corroborating prophecy and the religion's truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity of witnesses / martyrdom as credibility test
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I believe only the histories, whose witnesses got themselves killed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Willingness of witnesses to suffer or die for their testimony (martyrdom, preserving texts despite cost) is taken as strong evidence of sincerity and authenticity. Pascal cites Jews preserving their book and Maccabean witness as examples of credibility borne by costly fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneity of accounts and 'book that creates a nation'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is a great difference between a book which an individual writes, and publishes to a nation, and a book which itself creates a nation. Every history which is not contemporaneous... are false. It is not so with contemporaneous writers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounts written by contemporaries or narratives that form/organize a living people (a book that 'creates a nation') are more credible than later, non-contemporary histories or fabrications. Pascal uses this to argue for the trustworthiness of Mosaic and Jewish records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of inconvenient truths as sign of honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: 'They preserve lovingly and carefully the book in which Moses declares that they have been all their life ungrateful to God...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The continued preservation and transmission of texts that cast the preserving community in a negative light (self-condemning passages) indicate sincerity and authenticity rather than fabrication or propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genealogical complexity suggests non-concerted, authentic origin
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The genealogy of Jesus Christ in the Old Testament is intermingled with so many others that are useless, that it cannot be distinguished... What can be clearer than that this was not concerted?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent irregularities, interminglings, or 'useless' details (e.g., differing genealogies in Matthew and Luke) argue against collusion or later invention, and can be read as tokens of genuine historical transmission rather than crafted propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative prophetic credentials (foretoldness distinguishes true prophet)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The difference between Jesus Christ and Mahomet.--Mahomet was not foretold; Jesus Christ was foretold.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare claimants by whether their coming/role was foretold in prior, respected scriptures. Foretoldness (prophetic announcement) is used as a distinguishing criterion: a prophet whose arrival was predicted in earlier revelation is given stronger credence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting other religions that do not teach God's hiddenness
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If God were thus hidden, every religion which does not affirm that God is hidden, is not true; and every religion which does not give the reason of it, is not instructive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A true religion should acknowledge and account for the hiddenness/obscurity of God and explain its purpose; absence of that acknowledgement or explanation counts against a religion's truth and instructiveness in Pascal's view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear vs. obscure content as a comparative test (e.g., Koran vs Scripture)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is not by that which is obscure in Mahomet... that I would have him judged, but by what is clear... In that he is ridiculous. And since what is clear is ridiculous, it is not right to take his obscurities for mysteries.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing scriptures or prophetic claims, one should judge by the clear, manifest content (e.g., morally or intellectually absurd clear statements) rather than granting weight to obscure passages which might be post-hoc 'mysteries.' Clear absurdities undermine overall credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law's perfection, antiquity, and unbroken observance as divine sign
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The law by which this people is governed is at once the most ancient law in the world, the most perfect, and the only one which has been always observed without a break in a state.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A legal/religious code that is both ancient and has been continuously observed with notable rigor (even when severe) is presented as evidence of divine origin and as a reliable foundation for later revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longevity of patriarchs and close generational transmission as reliability test
rubrics_metrics.description: 'When men lived so long, children lived long with their parents... they conversed long with them. But what else could be the subject of their talk save the history of their ancestors... We see also that in these days tribes took particular care to preserve their genealogies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long lifespans in early genealogies and close intergenerational contact are argued to preserve historical memory and reduce the distortion of tradition, thus supporting the reliability of ancient accounts.
